summary: This document defines an immutable extension to the HTTP Cache-Control header. It tells a client that a response will not change during its freshness lifetime, so the client never has to revalidate it. That saves needless requests, for example when a user reloads a page.

eli5.summary: Some things never change, like a printed photo. This label tells your browser it does not need to keep asking whether the photo is the same.

questions: how to stop browsers revalidating cached files
is cache-control immutable safe over http
subtitle: A Cache-Control flag that tells browsers a fresh cached file will not change, so reloads can skip revalidation.

tldr.problem: Even when a cached response is still fresh, a user reload makes browsers send conditional requests for every sub-resource, and most come back as 304 Not Modified.
tldr.mechanism: A server adds the immutable Cache-Control extension to promise the response will not be updated during its freshness lifetime, so clients should not send conditional requests during that time.
tldr.outcome: Reloads stop wasting requests on resources published under versioned URLs. Clients should ignore the hint for non-HTTPS content and on force reloads.

today: RFC 8246 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2017. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the metadata for this site.

sections.title: The Problem With Reloads
sections.content:
HTTP's freshness lifetime lets a client reuse a stored response for a set time (see RFC 7234). The resource can still change during that time. A newspaper photo with a one-hour lifetime might be swapped at any moment, so different users see different photos until their caches expire.

Users who want to be sure press reload. That sends a conditional request (RFC 7232), and the server returns either a new representation or a 304 (Not Modified). A page with many dependent sub-resources can trigger hundreds of such requests.

Some sites never publish two variants of a sub-resource. They use versioned URLs: an updated file gets a new path, such as /101016/main.css becoming /102026/main.css, and links are updated at the same time. That allows a very large freshness lifetime, but the browser cannot tell this pattern is in use, so reloads still produce a wasted conditional request for each sub-resource.
sections.eli5: Imagine asking your teacher every morning whether yesterday's printed poster has changed, even though the school always hangs a brand new poster with a new number when something changes. The question is a waste of time.

sections.title: The immutable Extension
sections.content:
When present in a response, immutable indicates that the origin server will not update the representation of the resource during the freshness lifetime of the response. Clients SHOULD NOT issue a conditional request during that lifetime, for example upon a reload, unless the user explicitly overrides it, such as with a force reload.

The extension only applies while the stored response is fresh. Stale responses SHOULD be revalidated as usual. It takes no arguments; any arguments have no meaning and MUST be ignored. Several copies are equivalent to one, and the extension in a request has no effect.

Example from the RFC: Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable
sections.eli5: The server puts a sticker on the file that says it will not change until it expires. Your browser believes the sticker and stops double-checking.

sections.title: Intermediaries
sections.content:
An immutable response means the same thing to a proxy as to a user agent. Proxies SHOULD skip conditionally revalidating fresh responses that carry immutable, unless the client signals that validation is needed, for example with a no-cache request directive from RFC 7234.

A proxy that uses the extension to skip revalidation can choose whether to answer its own client with a 304 or a 200, based on the request headers it received.
sections.eli5: A helper in the middle who holds a copy can also trust the sticker, unless the person asking says to check anyway.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC describes immutable as a form of soft pinning. Like any pinning mechanism, it can amplify cache corruption incidents, including cache-poisoning attacks. It suggests three mitigations:

  • Clients SHOULD ignore the extension on resources that are not part of an authenticated context such as HTTPS.
  • Force-reload mechanisms, typically indicated through no-cache request attributes, SHOULD also ignore the extension, since they are used to repair interrupted loads and other corruption.
  • Clients SHOULD ignore it for resources without a strong indication that the stored size is correct, such as responses delimited by connection close.
sections.eli5: If a bad copy gets stuck in the cache, the sticker could keep it there. So browsers should only trust the sticker on safe connections and let a hard refresh override it.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: The immutable directive is registered in the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) Cache Directive Registry, following the guidelines in Section 7.1 of RFC 7234. The reference for the entry is RFC 8246.
sections.eli5: The new sticker name was written into the official list of allowed stickers.
